title: Safer Scripts with `set` Options 🛡️
description: Enable strict mode with -e, -u, and pipefail to catch errors before they become disasters.

slides.title: Why `set` Options? ⚙️
slides.content:
## Bash's Safety Switches

The `set` builtin lets you toggle shell behaviour. A few well‑chosen options drastically reduce bugs.

- `set -e` – exit immediately if a command fails.
- `set -u` – treat unset variables as an error.
- `set -o pipefail` – a pipeline fails if any part fails.

Together they are often called **strict mode**.

slides.title: The Magic Line
slides.content:
Start every script with:
```bash
set -euo pipefail
```

quizData.question: What does `set -e` do?

options.text: Exit immediately if a command returns non‑zero

quizData.explanation: `-e` (errexit) stops the script at the first failure.

slides.title: `set -u`: No More Typos 🔎
slides.content:
## Catch Uninitialised Variables

Without `-u`, a typo like `echo $config_file` (instead of `$config_file`) silently produces empty string. With `-u`, it's an error and the script halts.

Example:
```bash
set -u
echo $USER_NAME   # error if USER_NAME not set
```
Use `${var:-default}` to provide fallbacks safely.

slides.title: Fallback with -u
slides.content: Safe way to provide a default:

quizData.question: With `set -u`, `${varname:-default}` still works even if `varname` is not set.
quizData.explanation: The `:-` operator provides a default and does not trigger an unset error.

slides.title: `pipefail`: No Hiding Errors 🌊
slides.content:
## Whole Pipeline Integrity

Without `pipefail`, `false | true` returns 0 (success) because the last command succeeded. With `pipefail`, the pipeline returns 1.

```bash
set -o pipefail
false | true
echo $?   # 1
```
This prevents silent failures in long pipelines.

slides.title: pipefail Example
slides.content: Catch a failure in a pipe:
slides.codeSnippet:
set -o pipefail
cat nonexistent_file | wc -l
echo "Exit: $?"

slides.title: ⚠️ Caveats of `set -e`
slides.content: `set -e` has some surprising exceptions (e.g., commands in `if`, `while`, `&&`, `||`, or pipelines before the last command). Test your script thoroughly. Some developers prefer explicit error checks over `set -e`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `set -e` for new scripts, but if you're debugging an existing one, add it gradually. Combine with `trap` to log errors before exit.
